script:
Roth or traditional 401(k)? Here's how to pick.
Traditional comes out before tax, so you get the break now and pay tax on withdrawals.
Roth is the opposite. You pay tax now, and qualified withdrawals are tax-free.
Let's run one example.
You're single with $70,000 of taxable income, so you're in the 22% bracket.
You put $10,000 into a traditional 401(k), which saves you $2,200 in federal tax this year.
That $10,000 really costs you $7,800 of take-home pay.
Same $7,800 into a Roth.
Say both double by retirement.
Traditional gives you $20,000, but if you retire in the 12% bracket, you owe $2,400 and keep $17,600.
Roth turns your $7,800 into $15,600, and you keep all of it.
Flip it. If you retire in the 24% bracket, traditional leaves you $15,200, and Roth wins at $15,600.
So the rule is simple: lower bracket later, go traditional. Higher bracket later, go Roth.
To decide, ask yourself three things.
Is your bracket higher now than you expect in retirement?
Do you need the tax break now to hit your match without squeezing your paycheck?
Are your earnings likely to climb a lot?
The 2026 limit is $24,500 across both types combined, and it goes to $25,500 in 2027.
This ignores state tax, so do your own research.
Tell me your bracket in the comments, and if you're looking to grow your net worth, follow me.

sources.supports: Pre-tax 401(k) contributions are made with before-tax dollars; Roth 401(k) contributions are made with after-tax dollars; qualified Roth distributions are not taxed (account held at least 5 years and withdrawal on or after age 59½, disability, or death).

Traditional 401(k) withdrawals are taxed as ordinary income in retirement while contributions reduce current taxable income; qualified Roth 401(k) withdrawals are federally tax-free; in 2026 the $24,500 employee limit applies to pre-tax and Roth contributions combined; state tax treatment of withdrawals varies.
The 401(k) employee contribution limit rises to $25,500 for 2027, up from $24,500 for 2026.

2026 single filer brackets: 12% for taxable income $12,401 to $50,400, 22% for $50,401 to $105,700; marginal rate is the rate on your highest dollar of income. (The worked dollar math in the script is illustrative arithmetic on these brackets.)

Choice should be based on current versus future marginal tax rates; Roth tends to fit someone expecting a higher bracket later; traditional can fit someone in peak earning years or with tight cash flow who wants the employer match with less hit to take-home pay; Roth is generally better for heirs.
